synopsis: A terrain model describes ground shape, a digital elevation model is a grid of ground heights, a mesh represents surfaces with triangles, and simplified invisible collision proxies provide contact detection; the booklet also uses DEM for the unrelated discrete element method in soil physics [f13123, f13124, f13127, f13126]. Visual fidelity alone is insufficient for braking: neural scenes lack native collision surfaces, field-recording environments need explicit geometry and other simulation components, and a berm-edge error of tens of centimetres can corrupt stopping-distance tests [f3913, f3726, f3910]. Hybrid scenes can combine Gaussian appearance with invisible collision meshes, fill reconstruction holes with explicit geometry and enable terrain editing, whereas terrain edits in neural reconstructions were not demonstrated [f3818, f4284, f4283, f4231]. Practical evidence includes a 2025 quarry mesh optimized to 50,000 polygons, but reconstructed RadaRays meshes produced empty sensor frames and were too large to clean manually; the booklet found no validation of heavy-machine simulated braking distance on gravel, mud, ice or slopes [f3796, f5103, f13132]. Scenario standards remain incomplete for off-road terrain: OpenDRIVE covers haul roads but needs additional representations for dig faces, stockpiles and free terrain, OpenCRG fits haul-road surfaces rather than open terrain and had unverified status, and ASAM identified missing deformable-terrain and related concepts [f7158, f7159, f7160, f7195].
